name: MacDesk
title: MacDesk: A Desktop Experience for Android
tagline: A macOS-inspired desktop launcher for Android tablets and foldables, featuring floating windows, a glass dock, and a built-in file manager.
shortDescription: Developed a Kotlin and Jetpack Compose launcher that transforms Android tablets and foldables into a desktop-style workspace with a menu bar, customizable dock, window management, and integrated productivity apps.
overview: MacDesk reimagines the Android home screen as a desktop workspace inspired by macOS. It combines a top menu bar, translucent dock, desktop icons, floating application windows, and a Finder-style file manager. Built entirely in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, the launcher integrates image editing, media playback, application discovery, and system customization into a unified interface designed for tablets and foldable devices.
problem: Android tablets and foldables offer large displays, but their conventional launcher experience does not always provide the desktop-style organization, window management, and integrated file workflows expected from a productivity environment.
solution: Built a custom Android home launcher with desktop-inspired navigation, draggable and resizable application windows, a customizable dock, integrated file management, media tools, and persistent workspace settings. The implementation combines Compose-based UI components with Android storage APIs and system capabilities.
architecture: Android Home Activity → Jetpack Compose Desktop UI → MVVM / DesktopViewModel → Repositories and StateFlow → DataStore / Android System APIs → Window Engine and Built-in Applications
workflow: Set MacDesk as the default launcher → Initialize desktop settings and installed apps → Render menu bar, desktop and dock → Launch built-in apps in managed windows → Browse files, edit images or play media → Customize appearance and pinned apps → Persist settings using DataStore.
features: Custom Android home screen and desktop workspace
macOS-inspired menu bar with clock, Wi-Fi and battery indicators
Glass-style dock with pinned apps and running indicators
Desktop icons for applications and storage locations
Draggable, resizable and minimizable application windows
Window zooming and left/right screen tiling
Mouse, trackpad and touch context menus
Built-in Finder-style file manager with list and icon views
File sorting, image and video thumbnails, and folder management
Image viewer and editor with crop, rotate, flip and adjustments
Built-in audio and video player using Media3
Support for compatible ADW, Nova, Apex, GO and Atom icon packs
Customizable wallpaper, theme, dock, menu bar and window settings
Persistent preferences and pinned application configuration
Notification access integration and notification count
Adaptive window behaviour for compact screens and larger displays
highlights: Implemented a desktop-style Android launcher entirely in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
Built a custom window management engine with position, size, z-order, minimization and maximization state.
Used MVVM and StateFlow to coordinate desktop state and application interactions.
Persisted launcher customization and desktop configuration using Jetpack DataStore.
Integrated file browsing, image editing and media playback into a unified workspace.
Implemented a wallpaper-based glass effect using a pre-blurred bitmap to avoid continuous background blur processing.
Supported pointer interactions and touch-based long-press context menus.
Integrated Android storage access and optional system configuration for freeform window mode.
challenges: Managing multiple overlapping windows and keeping their positions, sizes and stacking order consistent.
Adapting desktop-oriented interactions to touchscreens, compact displays and foldable form factors.
Working within Android's restrictions on storage access and protected directories.
Integrating installed icon packs and mapping their icons to desktop and dock applications.
Balancing visual effects with rendering performance and battery efficiency.
Working around Android system restrictions on launching third-party applications in floating windows.
Handling notification access and optional secure system settings that require explicit user authorization.
lessonsLearned: A desktop environment requires coordinated window state, focus management and interaction handling rather than just a desktop-style UI.
StateFlow and MVVM help separate application state from composable UI components.
Android platform capabilities and OEM behaviour significantly affect desktop-style multitasking.
The Storage Access Framework provides a way to let users grant access to selected folders without unrestricted file access.
Precomputing visual effects can reduce repeated rendering costs.
Adaptive layouts and interaction patterns are essential when supporting tablets, foldables and phones.
futureImprovements: Improve compatibility with third-party applications in floating windows.
Expand testing across Android tablets, foldables and OEM desktop modes.
Improve window snapping, focus management and multitasking interactions.
Add more desktop customization and workspace organization options.
Refine accessibility, keyboard navigation and mouse interaction.
Improve file operations and compatibility with external storage devices.
Add automated tests for window management, settings persistence and UI interactions.
Optimize responsiveness and stability across different screen sizes.

name: Resumate
title: Resumate: AI-Assisted Resume Editor
tagline: Transform Word resumes into structured, editable documents using natural-language AI instructions.
shortDescription: Helped built a FastAPI-powered resume editor that parses DOCX documents into structured data, supports natural-language editing through Gemini, and exports clean Word documents.
overview: Resumate is a lightweight AI-assisted resume editing application designed to simplify resume updates. Users upload existing Word documents, which are parsed into a structured Pydantic model. They can then request changes using natural language, review and revert previous edits, and export the updated resume as a cleanly formatted DOCX file.
problem: Editing existing resumes often involves repetitive manual formatting, locating specific sections, rewriting bullet points, and preserving document structure across multiple revisions.
solution: Developed a document-processing and AI-assisted editing pipeline that converts uploaded resumes into structured data, applies targeted changes through Gemini or supported local editing operations, validates the resulting model, and renders the updated content into a downloadable Word document.
architecture: DOCX Upload → FastAPI Backend → Document Parser → Pydantic Resume Model → Gemini AI / Local Patcher → Validation → SQLite Persistence → DOCX Renderer → Export
workflow: Upload resume → Extract paragraphs and tables → Recognize resume sections → Build structured resume model → Submit natural-language edit → Apply and validate changes → Persist revision and audit snapshot → Preview or revert changes → Export updated DOCX.
features: Local patching for supported editing instructions
Extraction of content from paragraphs and tables
Revert to the previous successful edit
Export of updated resumes as DOCX documents
API health checks and Docker-based deployment
highlights: Separated document parsing, AI editing, persistence, and rendering into dedicated components.
Improved resume parsing to recognize additional section headings and preserve table content in document order.
Added handling for bullet-point cleanup and supported local editing operations.
Improved edit reliability by detecting unchanged results and surfacing AI failures instead of silently reporting success.
Integrated Gemini JSON responses with Pydantic validation.
Used SQLite audit snapshots to support reverting successful edits.
challenges: Parsing resumes with inconsistent headings, bullet formatting, and tables.
Preserving existing resume content while applying targeted AI-generated edits.
Handling incompatibilities between Gemini structured-output schemas and Pydantic model definitions.
Distinguishing successful edits from unchanged or failed AI responses.
Maintaining consistent resume data between parsing, persistence, editing, and document export.
lessonsLearned: Document parsing requires explicit handling of Word paragraphs, tables, and inconsistent formatting.
Structured output validation is essential when integrating language models into data-processing pipelines.
AI-generated edits should be checked for meaningful changes before being persisted.
Separating application services from database access makes individual components easier to maintain and replace.
Audit snapshots provide a straightforward foundation for reversible editing workflows.
futureImprovements: Support complex Word layouts, multi-column resumes, and text boxes.
Add side-by-side previews with explicit save and confirmation controls.
Implement authenticated user accounts and ownership-based access controls.
Improve concurrent editing and multi-user collaboration support.
Add more export formats and customizable resume templates.
Expand automated regression testing for parsing and AI editing.
Add integration tests for the complete upload-to-export workflow.

name: SSwavRecorder
title: SSwavRecorder, A Native Android WAV Audio Recorder
tagline: A lightweight Android audio recorder built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for capturing uncompressed WAV audio.
shortDescription: Developed a native Android audio recording application that captures uncompressed 16-bit PCM WAV audio at 44.1 kHz in mono, featuring live waveform visualization, background recording support, and recording recovery functionality.
overview: SSwavRecorder is a native Android application designed to provide straightforward WAV audio recording on devices where a dedicated WAV recording option may not be available. Built using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, the application records uncompressed 16-bit PCM audio at a sample rate of 44.1 kHz using a mono channel configuration. It combines a live waveform display with a foreground recording service to support recording while the application is in the background. Recording recovery functionality helps address interruptions, while the application uses Hilt and Room as part of its dependency injection and data persistence architecture.
problem: Many built-in smartphone recording applications prioritize compressed audio formats or do not expose a straightforward option for recording uncompressed PCM WAV audio. This can make it inconvenient for developers, audio enthusiasts, and technical projects that require predictable audio formats for processing, analysis, or experimentation.
solution: Developed a dedicated Android WAV recorder using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. The application captures mono audio as uncompressed 16-bit PCM at 44.1 kHz, displays a live waveform during recording, and uses a foreground service to support continued recording when the application moves into the background. Recovery functionality and structured application components help improve recording reliability and maintainability.
architecture: User Interface (Jetpack Compose) → Recording Controls → Audio Capture and PCM Processing → WAV File Output. Supporting Components: Foreground Recording Service → Background Recording Support; Hilt → Dependency Injection; Room → Local Data Persistence.
workflow: Launch application → Grant required microphone permissions → Start recording → Capture audio through Android audio APIs → Process audio as 16-bit PCM at 44.1 kHz, mono → Update the live waveform → Write audio data into a WAV file → Stop recording and finalize the file. Recovery mechanisms address supported recording interruptions.
highlights: Built a native Android application using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
Implemented WAV recording with a defined PCM audio format and sampling configuration.
Integrated live waveform visualization for real-time recording feedback.
Used a foreground service to support audio recording outside the active application screen.
Organized application components using Android development libraries including Hilt and Room.
Developed a practical utility that also supports audio experimentation and signal-processing projects.
challenges: Capturing audio and writing valid WAV files with the correct PCM format and audio metadata.
Keeping waveform visualization responsive while audio capture and file writing are in progress.
Managing microphone permissions and Android foreground-service requirements.
Handling recording interruptions and recovery without compromising the integrity of saved audio.
Coordinating UI state with recording operations and application lifecycle events.
lessonsLearned: Audio file formats require careful handling of sample rates, channel configurations, bit depth, and WAV headers.
Android audio recording involves lifecycle management and platform-specific permission requirements.
Foreground services are useful for supported long-running recording tasks when configured according to Android requirements.
Separating recording logic from UI components improves maintainability and testability.
Real-time waveform rendering requires balancing visual responsiveness with audio-processing workloads.
futureImprovements: Add configurable sample rates, channel counts, and recording formats.
Introduce audio playback and recording metadata displays.
Add recording duration, file size, and audio-level indicators.
Expand automated tests for recording interruptions and WAV file integrity.
Improve accessibility and support for different screen sizes.
Add export and sharing options for recorded audio files.
Explore integration with audio analysis and signal-processing workflows.

name: MangaAsari
title: MangaAsari — Manga Discovery & Chapter Aggregation
tagline: A multi-source manga discovery platform built around a canonical data model and idempotent chapter synchronization.
shortDescription: Built a Python-based manga discovery application integrating AniList and MangaDex with FastAPI, SQLite, and SQLAlchemy. Designed a source-agnostic data model that separates canonical manga and chapters from source-specific mappings and releases, enabling repeatable synchronization without duplicate records.
overview: MangaAsari is a manga discovery and chapter aggregation project developed to simplify finding manga and locating specific chapters across external sources. It uses AniList for manga search and metadata, while MangaDex provides source matching and chapter metadata. Users can select a chapter and navigate directly to its original MangaDex reader. The application maintains its own structured representation of manga, chapters, external sources, and source-specific releases rather than storing raw API responses. Built with Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and SQLAlchemy, the project explores maintainable backend architecture and provides a foundation for integrating additional manga sources through a shared interface.
problem: Finding a specific manga chapter can require searching across multiple websites and navigating different catalogues. From a software design perspective, integrating multiple sources also introduces data consistency challenges: the same manga or chapter may appear under different external identifiers, and a single chapter may have multiple releases from the same source. Treating every external release as a separate manga chapter would create duplicate records and make future source integration more difficult.
solution: Developed a backend that separates canonical manga and chapter entities from their source-specific representations. AniList provides manga discovery, while MangaDex is integrated through a dedicated source adapter. MangaSourceMapping connects canonical manga records to external manga identifiers, and ChapterSource associates canonical chapters with individual source releases. Chapter synchronization finds or creates the appropriate records and is designed to be idempotent, allowing repeated synchronization without creating duplicate entries. The application links users to the original MangaDex reader instead of hosting manga content.
architecture: Client Interface → FastAPI Application → Application Logic → AniList Integration / Manga Source Interface → MangaDex Adapter → External API Responses → Canonical Data Processing → SQLAlchemy ORM → SQLite Database. Data Model: Manga → MangaSourceMapping → Source; Manga → Chapter → ChapterSource → Source.
workflow: Search for a manga through AniList → Process its metadata and maintain a canonical manga record → Find or manually match the manga to an external source → Store the source-specific manga identifier → Fetch available chapter metadata through the source adapter → Match or create canonical chapter records → Associate each external release with its canonical chapter → Persist changes in SQLite → Let the user select a chapter and open its original MangaDex URL.
features: Multiple releases associated with one canonical chapter
Idempotent synchronization to prevent duplicate records
Direct navigation to original MangaDex chapter URLs
highlights: Designed a canonical data model that separates manga and chapter identities from their external source records.
Implemented source mapping to preserve external manga identifiers and avoid repeatedly searching for known source matches during synchronization.
Modeled chapter releases separately from canonical chapters, allowing multiple releases of the same chapter to coexist without creating duplicate canonical chapters.
Structured source integrations around a common MangaSource interface, with a dedicated MangaDex implementation and a mock source for development.
Designed chapter synchronization to be idempotent, so rerunning synchronization does not create duplicate records.
Processed a Detective Conan MangaDex feed containing 1,558 source chapter records, resulting in 1,168 canonical chapters because multiple releases can map to the same chapter.
Verified that a subsequent synchronization of the same feed added zero new chapters.
Integrated AniList and MangaDex while keeping chapter reading on the original source rather than implementing a proprietary reader.
challenges: Distinguishing a canonical chapter from individual releases published by external sources.
Representing manga and chapter relationships across multiple sources without coupling the database schema to one provider.
Maintaining reliable mappings between canonical manga records and external source identifiers.
Designing synchronization logic that can be repeated safely without creating duplicate records.
Reconciling chapter metadata when different releases from the same source may correspond to the same canonical chapter.
Keeping external API integration separate from the application's data model to support future source adapters.
lessonsLearned: Canonical entities and source-specific mappings provide a useful foundation for aggregating data from multiple external providers.
A chapter and a chapter release are different concepts and should be modeled separately when multiple releases can represent the same underlying chapter.
Idempotent synchronization makes recurring data ingestion safer and easier to reason about.
Persisting external identifiers allows applications to reuse known mappings instead of repeatedly searching remote services.
A shared source interface reduces coupling between application logic and individual API providers.
Structured local data models offer more control over relationships and consistency than storing raw external API responses alone.
Using original-source links can deliver useful aggregation functionality without building or hosting a separate content reader.
futureImprovements: Integrate additional manga sources through the existing source interface.
Improve automatic matching between manga across external catalogues.
Add user-selectable chapter languages.
Expand chapter filtering, sorting, and discovery controls.
Improve the user interface and overall discovery experience.
Introduce caching and more resilient handling of external API failures where appropriate.
Add automated tests for source adapters, database relationships, and synchronization idempotency.
Implement reading progress and chapter notifications.
Explore an Android application backed by the same multi-source architecture.
Evaluate applicable third-party API requirements before introducing an in-app reader or changing how external content is accessed.

name: FASECURE
title: FASECURE — Face Anti-Spoofing using CDCN++
tagline: A deep learning-based face anti-spoofing system capable of detecting print and replay attacks in real time.
shortDescription: Developed a real-time face anti-spoofing system using an enhanced CDCN++ architecture to distinguish genuine users from print and replay attacks through webcam inference.
overview: FASECURE is a deep learning-powered face anti-spoofing system developed to improve the security of facial authentication systems. The project implements an enhanced CDCN++ architecture integrated with Multi-Attentional Feature Maps (MAFM), Spoof Cue Map Generation, and Feature Fusion to identify spoofing attempts such as printed photographs and replay attacks. The trained model is deployed through a real-time webcam inference pipeline using OpenCV and PyTorch.
problem: Traditional face recognition systems can often be deceived using printed photographs or digital screen replays. Such presentation attacks compromise biometric authentication and create significant security risks in real-world applications.
solution: Designed and trained an enhanced CDCN++ model capable of learning spoof-specific texture patterns using Central Difference Convolution. The system combines attention mechanisms and feature fusion to improve representation learning and performs real-time inference using a webcam, accurately classifying faces as Live or Spoof.
architecture: Input Face → Face Detection (OpenCV SSD) → Image Preprocessing → Enhanced CDCN++ → Central Difference Convolution Layers → Multi-Attentional Feature Map (MAFM) → Spoof Cue Map Generation → Feature Fusion Module → Global Average Pooling → Binary Classification (Live / Spoof)
workflow: Capture webcam frame → Detect face using OpenCV SSD → Crop detected face → Resize and normalize image → Run inference through the trained CDCN++ model → Apply sigmoid activation → Display Live or Spoof prediction with confidence score on the video feed.
highlights: Implemented an enhanced CDCN++ architecture for face anti-spoofing.
Integrated Multi-Attentional Feature Maps to improve feature representation.
Designed a modular PyTorch implementation for training and inference.
Built a real-time webcam inference pipeline using OpenCV.
Organized the project with separate model, utility, resource, and inference modules for maintainability.
challenges: Implementing research concepts from the CDCN++ architecture into a practical application.
Maintaining real-time inference performance while preserving detection accuracy.
Handling face detection reliability under varying lighting conditions.
Managing model compatibility across different PyTorch and OpenCV versions.
lessonsLearned: Research papers often require practical adaptations before production implementation.
Modular project organization significantly improves maintainability and deployment.
Computer vision models rely heavily on preprocessing consistency.
Model optimization and inference pipelines are equally important as model training.
futureImprovements: Extend support for mask and 3D presentation attacks.
Train using larger public face anti-spoofing datasets.
Deploy as a web application using FastAPI or Flask.
Optimize inference for edge devices.
Add liveness visualization through spoof heatmaps.
Support ONNX and TensorRT deployment.

name: Artscii
title: Artscii — ASCII Art Generator
tagline: Convert images into expressive ASCII art with a lightweight desktop application.
shortDescription: Built a Python-based application that converts images into ASCII art by mapping pixel brightness to printable character sets with adjustable output quality.
overview: Artscii is a simple image processing application that transforms ordinary images into text-based ASCII artwork. The project demonstrates grayscale conversion, pixel intensity analysis, character mapping, and configurable rendering to generate visually recognizable ASCII representations.
problem: Creating readable ASCII art manually is time-consuming and requires careful character placement. Automating the process requires efficient image preprocessing and brightness-to-character mapping.
solution: Implemented an image-to-ASCII conversion pipeline that preprocesses images, converts them to grayscale, scales them while preserving aspect ratio, and maps pixel intensities to ordered ASCII characters to generate high-quality text art.
architecture: Image Input → Resize → Grayscale Conversion → Pixel Intensity Analysis → Character Mapping → ASCII Rendering → Text Output
workflow: Load image → Resize while preserving aspect ratio → Convert to grayscale → Map each pixel intensity to an ASCII character → Render and export the generated ASCII artwork.
highlights: Designed an efficient pixel-to-character mapping algorithm.
Implemented image preprocessing for cleaner ASCII output.
Maintained image proportions during conversion.
Produced lightweight text-based artwork from ordinary images.
challenges: Balancing detail and readability in ASCII output.
Preserving aspect ratio despite differing character dimensions.
Selecting character sets that produce visually pleasing results.
lessonsLearned: Small image-processing techniques significantly impact visual quality.
Character selection is critical for realistic ASCII rendering.
Aspect ratio correction is essential when converting images to text.
futureImprovements: Support colored ASCII output.
Allow custom character sets.
Export HTML and ANSI formats.
Batch image conversion.
